title: Plum Pocket Disease (Taphrina pruni, Ascomycota Taphrinaceae) on European and Japanese Plum
content: Plum pocket (also called plum bladder, plum bladder plum, or swollen plum) is a distinctive spring fungal disease of European plum (Prunus domestica L.) and Japanese plum (P. salicina Lindl.) and their interspecific plum hybrids (P. domestica x P. salicina, P. americana x P. salicina). It is caused by the dimorphic ascomycete Taphrina pruni (Fuckel) Tul. (subphylum Taphrinomycotina, class Taphrinomycetes, order Taphrinales, family Taphrinaceae), closely related to T. deformans (peach leaf curl), T. communis (cherry leaf curl), and T. bullata (pear leaf blister). Plum pocket occurs in all cool temperate plum-growing regions of North America (northeastern and northwestern US, southern Canada), northern and central Europe (United Kingdom, France, Germany, Poland, Ukraine, Russia), northern China, Japan, Chile, Argentina, and New Zealand; it is most severe in orchards located in cool, foggy river valleys and high-rainfall areas during spring, and usually occurs only sporadically in warm dry years. Yield losses of 10-60% are recorded in highly susceptible plum cultivars in years with cool wet spring weather; additional losses occur due to the complete inedibility of infected fruit (pocketed fruit are hollow, tasteless, and contain no functional seed or edible flesh). The disease also occasionally affects the young leaves and succulent shoots of plum and, rarely, of apricot (P. armeniaca) and cherry plum (P. cerasifera). The diagnostic and most economically important symptom of plum pocket occurs on developing young plum fruit within 3-6 weeks after fruit set: infected fruit develop abnormally, becoming enlarged, elongated, spongy, hollow, bladder- or pocket-shaped structures (3-8 cm long, up to 10x the size of healthy fruit) that are light green to yellowish-green with a smooth or slightly wrinkled surface; the infected fruit structure is called a 'pocket' or 'bladder' (Latin 'ascus' derivative). The characteristic pockets lack a normal stony endocarp (pit or stone) and contain no functional embryo, seed, or edible mesocarp flesh; the entire interior of the pocket is empty or contains only a thin, dry, fibrous, abortive remnant of the seed and endocarp. Approximately 10-14 days after the first appearance of pocket symptoms, the surface of the bladder-like pocket develops a grayish, velvety, powdery bloom covering the entire exterior surface; this bloom consists of a palisade layer of naked asci (ascogenous hymenium) of T. pruni, similar to that produced by T. deformans on curled peach leaves. After the ascospore discharge, the pockets turn brown, wither, and either hang on the tree as dry, wrinkled, dark mummified structures for the remainder of the summer, or drop from the tree prematurely in early summer. In addition to fruit pockets, T. pruni also causes less frequently observed symptoms on young plum leaves and new shoots: infected young leaves are thickened, distorted, curled, and develop a reddish-purple to silvery gray discoloration (often confused with the early stages of powdery mildew or plum pox virus infection); infected young shoots are swollen, thickened, stunted, and curled into 'witches' broom'-like clusters. Heavily infected branches may die back in late summer, providing entry courts for perennial Cytospora leucostoma and Leucostoma persoonii canker fungi. Taphrina pruni is a strict dimorphic parasite with a life cycle nearly identical to that of T. deformans (peach leaf curl): (1) saprotrophic haploid yeast-like budding blastospore stage overwinters epiphytically on the surface of bark, within bud scales, and in bark crevices of 1-2 year-old plum wood; (2) in early spring during the period from plum bud swell (white bud stage) through bloom (petal fall) and initial fruit set, rain and dew splash the overwintered blastospores onto the surfaces of newly emerging, tender, young ovary tissue, floral primordia, and young leaf primordia; (3) compatible haploid blastospores conjugate via a short conjugation tube to form dikaryotic infection hyphae that penetrate the thin unprotected cuticle of the still-undifferentiated young ovary wall (the infection court for fruit symptoms closes very rapidly after successful pollination and fertilization of the ovule, which is why severe pocket years are invariably associated with extended cool rainy periods during bloom that delay fertilization and keep the young ovary cuticle thin and susceptible for a longer period); (4) once inside the ovary wall, the dikaryotic mycelium grows intercellularly throughout the developing pericarp, inducing massive hyperplasia (excessive cell division) and hypertrophy (cell enlargement) of the mesocarp tissue while simultaneously suppressing normal differentiation and lignification of the endocarp (pit) and embryo/seed development - resulting in the hollow, bladder-like pocket structure with no stony pit; (5) approximately 3 weeks after infection, the dikaryotic mycelium reaches the fruit surface, karyogamy (nuclear fusion) occurs in subepidermal cells, and a naked palisade hymenium of club-shaped asci (50-100 x 10-18 um) containing 8 (rarely 4) ellipsoidal haploid ascospores (5-9 x 3-6 um) forms directly on the pocket surface (the gray velvety bloom); (6) ascospores are forcibly discharged during rain events in late spring and are wind- and splash-dispersed back onto the bark surface and newly formed bud scales, where they immediately convert back to the saprotrophic yeast-like budding stage that will survive the following dormant season; (7) as with all Taphrina diseases, there is only ONE primary infection cycle per growing season, no secondary fruit reinfection occurs in summer even under extended wet conditions, so disease incidence for the year is entirely determined by weather conditions during the short 2-3 week window of bud swell through petal fall. Infection requires 18-48 hours of continuous free moisture (rain, dew, fog drip) on the bud and young fruit surface at temperatures of 7-19 C (45-66 F); incidence above 25% generally requires > 50 mm of rainfall distributed across the 3-week bloom period. Plum cultivar susceptibility differs dramatically: highly susceptible European plum varieties include 'Stanley' (the most susceptible cultivar in North American and European trials), 'Italian Prune' (Prune d'Ente), 'President', 'Reine Claude' (Green Gage), 'Damas', and 'Quetsche'; highly susceptible Japanese plum cultivars include 'Santa Rosa', 'Burbank', 'Formosa', 'Shiro', and 'Satsuma'. Moderately resistant or tolerant cultivars include European 'Agen', 'Valor', 'Violetta', 'Hall', 'Ruth Gerstetter'; Japanese 'Black Amber', 'Friar', 'Angeleno', 'Fortune'. Management: because of the short infection window and the single-cycle nature of the disease, the management program for plum pocket is very similar to that for peach leaf curl and relies primarily on dormant fungicide sprays: (1) a single, properly timed dormant fungicide application applied in late autumn after 95% leaf fall OR in early spring at the delayed dormant / 'silver tip' to 'white bud' stage (BEFORE any green or pink tissue emerges from the bud scales) provides 90-99% control. The most effective materials are lime sulfur (calcium polysulfide, 6-8% v/v dilute, 25-40 g sulfur / L) and Bordeaux mixture (8:8:100 or 10:10:100 CuSO4:lime:water), both permitted in certified organic production. Fixed copper formulations (copper hydroxide, copper oxychloride, tribasic copper sulfate) at 2-3 lb metallic Cu per acre provide equivalent efficacy and cause less dormant-season bark phytotoxicity on sensitive Japanese plum cultivars. (2) post-bloom foliar sprays are generally NOT effective for fruit pocket control because the ovary infection court is closed immediately after pollination and fertilization; however, if a dormant spray was forgotten, foliar sprays of FRAC 3 DMI triazoles (tebuconazole, propiconazole, myclobutanil, difenoconazole) + FRAC M3 mancozeb tank-mix applied at white bud, first bloom, and petal fall may reduce pocket incidence by 50-70% under moderate pressure, but are unreliable under high-inoculum, wet-year conditions. (3) cultural practices: remove and destroy (burn, landfill, hot-compost) any pocketed fruit and pocketed witches' broom shoots as soon as they are first observed in early summer (BEFORE the gray ascospore bloom develops on the pocket surface); this practice does not eliminate already-established bark inoculum, but reduces local inoculum levels the following year, particularly effective in young orchards still building up T. pruni inoculum. Prune for open, well-ventilated tree architecture to accelerate spring drying of the blossom and fruit zone. (4) genetic resistance: avoid planting large contiguous monoculture blocks of highly susceptible cultivars such as 'Stanley', 'Italian Prune', or 'Santa Rosa' in cool, foggy, high-spring-rainfall orchard sites. Where plum pocket is a chronic annual problem, plant the moderately resistant cultivars listed above. (5) orchard site selection: avoid planting plums on low-lying, poorly air-drained frost pocket sites, in close proximity to native wild P. americana (American plum) thickets which serve as a perennial wild reservoir of T. pruni inoculum, or in cool north-facing slopes where spring temperatures remain cool and dew/fog periods are extended through the bloom period.
